newsitem.title: USA: Princes Di gown seen worth $10 million as 'jewelry'.
newsitem.headline: Princes Di gown seen worth $10 million as 'jewelry'.

text.p: It's a dress that sold for $34,500 just last month at a Christie's auction in New York. But soon, the beaded silk gown once worn by Princess Diana could be worth $10 million.

Roxanne Duke, who bought the dress at Christie's, says that what attracted her to the pleated cream-coloured garment was the more than 20,000 beads and imitation pearls used to create a delicate floral pattern on its bodice and sleeves.
"This particular one is good for what we wanted to do," Duke, an owner of the family-run International Gem, Mineral and Jewelry Show Inc., told Reuters in an interview on Friday.
What the Duke family wanted to do, simply put, was to turn a dress once owned by British royalty into designer earrings for American consumers -- 10,000 pairs of earrings, to be exact.
"We plan to take some of the pearls off and make earrings. The earrings would sell for $1,000 a pair," she said.
That would amount to $10 million in gross sales, or about three times the $3.2 million which Christie's raised by selling 79 of Princess Diana's old gowns.
The Dukes' plan has been blasted by British tabloids which say the Americans are out to destroy the gown, which Diana wore in London in 1982 and again on a visit to Nepal in 1993.
"They've accused us of wanting to 'cannibalize' the dress," Duke said in Atlanta, where the gown went on display as part of a jewelry show organised by her family's Rockville, Maryland-based company.
But Roxanne and her brother, Arnold, say destroying the dress could not be further from their minds.

Their plan calls for the family business to absorb the cost of buying the dress and converting the beads into earrings. All $10 million in sales proceeds then could go to beneficiaries like the cancer and AIDS charities helped by the Christie's auction.
"Because we are continuing her goodwill, I think it's a good idea. We're kind of following her wishes," Roxanne said.

Besides, fake pearls used for earrings could be replaced, and the dress could go back on display alongside a ruby crown that belonged to Princess Michael of Kent and a pair of Romanov wedding crowns from Russia.

The Dukes have contacted palace officials in London to find out if their plans would be alright with Diana herself. "Her personal assistant said she has sold the dress and that we are now the new owners. So, it's really our decision," she said.
The family also hopes to ask the dress designer Catherine Walker for help in removing and replacing the original beads.
"The business we're in is running gem and jewelry shows, and the public loves to see what kind of jewelry Marilyn Monroe might have worn, or Elvis Presley," said Arnold Duke.
"We display it and occasionally we sell it ... for example, we are now selling some of Jackie Kennedy Onassis' jewelry," he said.
Roxanne expects a lot of demand for earrings made from Diana's dress, because the British royal has never sold her jewelry to the public.

"The auction was such an exciting event, and so many people would have loved to own a dress or something that belonged to Diana," she said. "This way, people can actually afford to own something that belonged to her."

The first earrings from the dress were not expected to appear before the end of the year. The Dukes said they would send the gown on a six-month tour of the United States first, during which time they would pick an earring designer and prepare for the task of removing the beads.
To guarantee authenticity, customers would get certificates and photos of beads being cut from the dress for each pair of earrings.
